catalog_quote: Stress placement in Wambaya is sensitive to morphological structure; each polysyllabic morpheme constitutes a new domain for the placement of stress. Generally stress falls on the first syllable of the stress domain and on each following alternate syllable, except that the final syllable usually does not carry any stress. Stress placement is also sensitive to syllable weight as heavy syllables (i.e. those containing a phonemic long vowel) are always stressed whether they are in the first or second syllable of the stress domain (the only two positional possibilities for long vowels). Therefore, with the exception of a handful of words with a phonemic long vowel in their second syllable, primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word. (p.33) ... Phonemic long vowels always receive primary stress irrespective of their position in the word ... Long vowels as in (a) to (d) above howe…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, unless the second syllable holds a phonemic long vowel, in which case that syllable takes primary stress (p. 33; p. 24: 'Phonemic long vowels always receive primary stress irrespective of their position in the word', e.g. ga'rnaa 'long', ngi'rnii 'south', ga'laa 'bone', ga'rdaala 'gidgee tree'; p. 35: Nga.'naa.rra, ga.'laa, ga.'rdaa.la). Long vowels can only stand in the first or second syllable of a stress domain, so the window is bounded at the left edge; heavy = phonemic long vowel only (closed syllables such as garn., jam., bung. are not heavy, Table 2.4 p. 34). Formalised on pp. 34-36 as left-headed, quantity-sensitive binary feet built left to right per morpheme, then grouped into a left-branching word tree (rule (v)). The rules are explicitly modelled on Nash (1986) for Warlpiri (p. 33).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, described in detail. Each polysyllabic morpheme is a separate stress domain; within a domain stress falls on the first syllable and on every following alternate syllable, the final syllable usually unstressed (p. 33). Monosyllabic suffixes cannot form a domain: they pair with a following monosyllabic suffix into a disyllabic domain, or else join the root's domain; monosyllabic roots are their own domain; the auxiliary is its own domain only if polysyllabic, a monosyllabic auxiliary attaches to the word to its left ('bung.ma.+,nya.=ga, pp. 33-34). Table 2.4 p. 34 gives e.g. 'bu.lyu.,ngu+rna 'little+II', 'ngu.rra.,ram.ba+ni 'night-time+LOC', 'jam.ba+n.,man.ji 'ground+ALL', 'da.gu.maj.+,ba.rli 'hit+AGNT', jany.+,bu.lu 'dog+DU'.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) p. 33 fn. 23: 'In this respect I disagree with Chadwick (e.g. 1978:17) who claims that primary stress in all of the West Barkly languages falls on the penultimate syllable of the word.' (2) p. 24 and p. 37: phonetic long vowels created by elision of /w/ (e.g. darranggu+wulu > /darranggu+ulu/, tree+DU) do NOT take primary stress; only phonemic long vowels do; stress assignment precedes elision. (3) p. 38: 'The rules of stress placement in Wambaya are still not yet fully understood and further research may lead to a different analysis of stress placement than presented here. While the rules for foot and word construction given here account for the large majority of the corpus, there are some unpredictable forms that these rules do not account for.' Two listed: 'wug.ba.,rdij.+ba.,rli.+rna (expected 'wug.ba.rdij.+,ba.rli.+rna) 'cook+AGNT+II' and 'na.nga.na.,nga.li (expected 'na.nga.,na.nga.li) 'sneak away'; both concern secondary-stress placement, primary stress stays initial. (4) Long vowels are 'very rare in Wambaya' (p. 35), so the peninitial case is marginal.
new_statements.identity_note: Nordlinger's stress description is of Wambaya proper (her own corpus, Barkly Tableland, NT). Glottolog wamb1258 also spans the closely related varieties Gudanji and Binbinka; Nordlinger p. 24 notes a dialect difference relevant to stress: where Wambaya has a phonemic long vowel with peninitial primary stress (ga'rnaa 'long', ga'laa 'bone', ga'rdaala 'gidgee tree'), Gudanji keeps the semivowel and stresses the initial syllable ('garnawa, 'galawa, 'garda,wala), so in Gudanji the peninitial case does not arise. Chadwick's penultimate statement is a family-level claim for the West Barkly languages (Jingulu, Ngarnka, Wambaya, Gudanji, Binbinka) exemplified from Jingulu only.

readall_conflicts: One second-hand disagreement, already flagged by the source itself: Nordlinger 1998:33 fn. 23 rejects Chadwick's (1978:17) claim that primary stress in all West Barkly languages is penultimate. Chadwick's 1979 survey 'The West Barkly languages: an outline sketch' (PL C-54, already held by the project in this folder, opened by an earlier reading, not in this task's work list) states at sec. 3.1 p. 659: 'Stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word-unit. There are few exceptions. With the addition of suffixes to a stem, stress moves to the penultimate vowel of the series of suffixes', illustrated only with Djingili (Jingulu) forms. So for Wambaya the sources conflict: Chadwick (1978, 1979) = penultimate for the family as a whole, Nordlinger (1998, the only dedicated Wambaya grammar, corpus-based with a formal foot analysis) = initial with phonemic long vowels attracting primary stress. Nordlinger's detailed, language-specific account with marked examples (Table 2.4, pp. 21-24 transcriptions) outweighs Chadwick's one-line family-wide generalisation exemplified from Jingulu; the catalog's weight-sensitive / initial-default coding follows Nordlinger. Bender 2008 is silent.

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the standard reference grammar (Nordlinger 1998, PL C-140), which we hold; every segment of the deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim at the cited pages (p.33 rule statement, p.24 phonemic long vowels always primary-stressed, p.35 rule (iii), p.38 caveat). The classification (weight-sensitive, left edge, heavy = CVV with phonemic long vowel only, morpheme-based stress domains) matches the source exactly, including the author's own hedge that the analysis is provisional.
